newsitem.title: ALBANIA: EU states move closer to Albania security force.
newsitem.headline: EU states move closer to Albania security force.

text.p: Six EU states pushed closer on Wednesday to forming a multinational security force for strife-torn Albania to protect humanitarian workers and planned aid shipments, diplomats said.
Military experts from the EU countries scouted Albania to prepare for the possible security force, which is expected to be announced within days and to number in the hundreds.
"The team is made up of experts from all fields which could be involved in any kind of military operation," said an EU diplomat, who asked for anonymity.

A separate international relief mission arrived on Wednesday to discuss how to help end anarchy in the Balkan state -- divided by an armed insurrection in the south and bedevilled by daily random violence by heavily-armed outlaw gangs.

The delegation, comprising the EU and other groups and led by Dutch diplomat Jan de Marchant et d'Ansembourg, is due to meet Prime Minister Bashkim Fino and other ministers on Thursday to discuss the unrest in which more than 100 people have died since mid-January.
Violence swept Albania after several popular but fraudulent investment schemes failed, wiping out millions of dollars in savings across the country of 3.4 million people.
The protests grew into an armed revolt against President Sali Berisha, who lost control of the south where scores of lawless gangs now terrorise the population.
Rebels or criminal gangs control Albania from Vlore on the Adriatic coast to the Greek border in the south. Violence, theft and settling of scores has become daily fare.
A policeman was shot dead in Burrel, north of Tirana on Tuesday -- the fifth policeman killed this week, the state news agency ATA said.
Fino met local officials from around Albania on Wednesday and said his unity government was trying to secure more police equipment.

Police from Tirana to the Greek border fled in the face of this month's popular uprising. Their equipment was stolen or burned by enraged protesters, who moved on to loot thousands of weapons from army munitions depots.
The rightist Berisha appointed Fino, an opposition socialist, this month to head the new government in a desperate bid to cling to power.
Berisha also agreed to elections in June, three years early, but Albania is in desperate need of relief aid before then.
Fino told the officials that restoration of order and calm was the key step towards normalising life and clearing the way for substantial emergency aid.
The visiting EU military experts came from Italy, France, Portugal and Spain -- who make up the Florence-based Eurofor force -- as well as Austria and Greece.

In Vienna, the 54-member Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) was close to agreeing a framework for a broad international military force, made up of volunteer nations, diplomatic sources said.
The EU has shunned forming a security force for Albania but has said individual members could do so and advised them to find an appropriate international aegis for action.
Under the present draft plan the OSCE would serve as the umbrella group, and determine the mandate, diplomats said. Other states which might join the EU countries include Turkey and Romania.

While foreign countries ponder a security force, daily violence has plagued Albania. With Berisha's forces unable to re-establish control over the south, rebels have formed their own defiant town councils.

With rebel strongholds located near to the border, Albanian secret police chief Bashkim Gazidede accused groups in neighbouring Greece of plotting to "liberate" the south and said this was behind the present insurrection.

He told parliament on Wednesday that a plot called "Lotos" had been agreed by groups in Greece in 1990 for the liberation of southern Albania from Tirana's domination through an armed insurrection. This was now being implemented point by point.

So far the southern rebels have made no calls for autonomy or separation from Albania. At one point they threatened to set up a rival government to oppose Berisha, blamed for the failed investment schemes, but never carried this out.
